Kennewick Roofing: Repair and Replacement Built for Desert Sun and Wind

Roofs in Kennewick don't fail the way they do on the west side of the state. With only seven to eight inches of rain a year, rot and moss are rarely the enemy here. What kills roofs in the Tri-Cities is ultraviolet exposure and wind. Summer surface temperatures on a dark asphalt roof regularly pass 150°F, cooking the oils out of shingles until they curl and crack. Then the wind arrives — gusts funneling down the Columbia and across the open shrub-steppe routinely top 40 mph, and a shingle that's lost its flexibility loses its grip.

Roofing in Kennewick: what to know

That combination means Kennewick homeowners often see failures on roofs that would still be fine in Seattle: cracked and cupped shingles on the south-facing slope, lifted tabs along ridge lines, and granule loss that shows up as bald patches near gutters. A roofer who works this market knows to check wind ratings on replacement shingles, to look hard at the south and west exposures first, and to price tear-offs with local landfill fees in mind.

Whether you own a 1950s ranch near downtown that's carrying its third layer of composition shingle or a newer two-story in Southridge with architectural shingles approaching their 20-year mark, we can connect you with a Kennewick-area roofing contractor for an inspection and a written quote.

Common roofing situations in Kennewick

South-slope shingle burnout

The south-facing slope of a Kennewick roof takes brutal UV load with almost no cloud cover from June through September. Shingles on that exposure often age five to ten years faster than the north slope, so a roof can be simultaneously fine and failing. A good inspection evaluates each slope separately rather than quoting a blanket age.

Wind-lifted tabs and ridge caps

When spring winds push through the Horse Heaven Hills, the first casualties are ridge caps and the tab edges of aging three-tab shingles. One lifted tab lets wind get under its neighbors, and damage spreads in a fan pattern. Catching it after a wind event — before the next one — is the cheapest repair you'll ever schedule.

Flashing failure around swamp coolers and vents

Plenty of older Kennewick homes carry roof-mounted evaporative coolers or abandoned cooler curbs. The flashing around these penetrations dries out and splits in desert heat, and because rain is rare, the leak may not show until a February ice melt sends water into the attic all at once.

How it works

  1. 1

    Slope-by-slope inspection

    A roofer walks the roof or flies a drone over it, documenting each slope separately — shingle condition, flashing, penetrations, and decking softness — with photos you keep.

  2. 2

    Written scope and wind-rating spec

    You get a line-item quote naming the shingle product and its wind rating (look for 110–130 mph class shingles here), underlayment type, and whether decking replacement is priced per sheet.

  3. 3

    Tear-off or overlay decision

    Washington code allows up to two layers of composition shingle. If you're at two, tear-off is mandatory and disposal costs are part of the quote. If you're at one, the contractor should explain the trade-offs rather than defaulting to the cheaper overlay.

  4. 4

    Installation and cleanup

    Most Kennewick reroofs finish in one to three days. Magnetic nail sweeps of the yard and driveway should be in the contract — post-war neighborhoods here have mature landscaping where dropped nails hide well.

What roofing costs in Kennewick

Roof replacement in Kennewick typically runs on the cost of the shingle class, roof complexity, and tear-off layers. A simple gable ranch of 1,500–1,800 square feet with one tear-off layer sits at the affordable end; two-story Southridge homes with hips, valleys, and steep pitches cost meaningfully more per square. Wind-rated architectural shingles cost more upfront than basic three-tab but are the sensible spec in this wind zone — many local roofers won't warranty three-tab here anymore. Summer scheduling fills fast because crews avoid tear-offs during 100°F-plus stretches; shoulder-season bids in spring and fall are often sharper.

Frequently asked questions

How long do asphalt shingles actually last in Kennewick?

Expect the short end of the manufacturer's range. A '30-year' architectural shingle often delivers 18–24 years here because UV and thermal cycling age the south and west slopes fast. Lighter shingle colors and proper attic ventilation both stretch that lifespan.

Does my roofer need to be registered in Washington?

Yes. Washington requires contractors to register with the Department of Labor & Industries, carry a bond, and carry liability insurance. You can verify any contractor's registration number free on the L&I website before signing anything.

Is metal roofing worth it in the Tri-Cities?

Metal performs well here — it shrugs off UV, sheds wind, and reflects summer heat, which can trim cooling bills. The upfront cost is roughly double asphalt, so it pencils out best if you plan to stay in the home 15+ years or want to stop thinking about the roof entirely.

Will my homeowners insurance cover wind damage to my roof?

Most Washington policies cover sudden wind damage, but insurers distinguish between wind damage and wear. A roof that lost tabs at 25 years old may get a depreciated payout or a denial. Document damage with dated photos right after a wind event and get an inspection before filing.

What time of year is best to reroof in Kennewick?

April–June and September–October are ideal. Shingles seal properly in moderate temperatures, crews are not fighting 105°F deck heat, and you avoid the winter weeks when adhesive strips may not bond until a warm spell.
